items.name: OpenAI API
items.about: I use the OpenAI API where a product needs output it can trust. In the AI form builder, a constrained prompt returns a strict JSON schema, and the server validates it before anything renders.
uses: Structured output, validated on the server
Prompts tuned for a predictable token cost
Cached results so a repeat request costs nothing

items.name: Claude API
items.about: I build with the Claude API for reading and writing tasks inside SaaS products, behind the same guardrails I use for every model: server-side calls, validation, rate limits and token caps.
uses: Keys stay on the server, never in the browser
Per-tenant rate limits and token caps
Typed, validated responses before anything is stored

items.name: RAG
items.about: Retrieval-augmented generation lets a model answer from a customer’s own data. I keep retrieval tenant-aware, so one customer’s documents never reach another customer’s answers.
uses: Answers that point back to their source

items.name: Agents
items.about: I build agents as small, observable steps with clear limits on what each tool may do, so every run can be traced, capped and stopped.
uses: Step and cost limits per run
A log line for every step

items.name: MCP
items.about: Model Context Protocol servers give an AI client a typed, permissioned way into a product’s data and actions. I build them on the product’s own API, with the same access rules.
uses: MCP servers over an existing API
Auth that matches the product’s roles

items.name: Token and cost controls
items.about: AI features get expensive quietly. I put server-side token caps, caching and per-tenant budgets in place so AI cost stays flat as usage grows, as in the AI form builder.
uses: Token caps per request and per tenant

items.name: tiktoken (token validation)
items.about: tiktoken counts tokens the same way OpenAI models do, so the server can check a prompt against its cap before the request is sent and paid for.
uses: Counting tokens before a model call
Rejecting oversized prompts on the server
Budgets that match what the provider bills

items.name: Cursor
items.about: I use Cursor every day. I also take over apps that were mostly written in it, and the audit starts with what it tends to skip: tenancy, rate limits and error handling.
uses: Week-one audit of a Cursor-written codebase
Tests around the parts that touch money and data

items.name: v0
items.about: v0 produces good-looking Next.js screens fast. I connect those screens to a real backend with auth, data isolation and payments.
uses: v0 components turned into a maintainable Next.js app
Real data and auth behind the UI

items.name: Bolt
items.about: Bolt gets a full-stack prototype running in minutes. I add what a paying customer needs: security, multi-tenancy and payments that reconcile.
uses: Moving a Bolt prototype into a real repo and pipeline

items.name: Lovable
items.about: Lovable apps usually sit on Supabase. Before real users arrive I add row-level security, server-side validation and separate environments.
uses: Payments and webhooks that survive retries

items.name: ChatGPT code
items.about: Code pasted from ChatGPT often works on its own and breaks in context. Taking over code an AI tool wrote is most of my work: I read it, audit it and keep what works.
uses: Reading and mapping the whole codebase first
A written risk report before any rewrite
Fixes in order of what breaks first

items.name: React
items.about: React is the front end of almost every system on this site: the creator platform, the immigration portal, the quote engine, the video dashboard and the fantasy sports platform.
uses: Responsive layouts for desktop, tablet and phone

items.name: Next.js
items.about: I use Next.js for SaaS products that need server rendering, API routes and good SEO. The AI form builder runs on it.

items.name: JavaScript
items.about: JavaScript is what every project here runs on, in the browser and on Node.js, and where I debug most production issues.
uses: Modern ES modules and async code
Browser APIs for camera, media and location
Debugging across browser, API and database

items.name: TypeScript
items.about: I write new code in TypeScript and add types to inherited JavaScript as I go, starting with the parts that handle money and user data.
uses: Typed API contracts between front end and back end
Gradual typing of an existing codebase

items.name: HTML and CSS
items.about: Semantic HTML and plain CSS come first: responsive pages that work on desktop, tablet and phone, and forms anyone can use with a keyboard. This site is hand-built in both.

items.name: Tailwind CSS
items.about: Tailwind for fast, consistent UI work, mapped to a design system’s tokens rather than one-off values.
uses: Design tokens in the Tailwind theme
Shared components instead of copied classes
Dark and light themes from one set of tokens

items.name: Redux Toolkit
items.about: Redux Toolkit keeps shared client state predictable in larger React apps, with slices, async thunks and one place to look when state goes wrong.
uses: Normalised state for lists and caches

items.name: Node.js
items.about: Node.js runs my backends: the creator platform’s payout webhooks, the quote engine’s APIs, the video pipeline’s Lambda functions and the fantasy platform’s real-time server.
uses: Webhook handlers that are safe to retry

items.name: Express
items.about: Express when I want a small, explicit server: routing, validation, auth middleware and error handling I can read in one sitting.

items.name: REST APIs
items.about: I design and consume REST APIs and integrate third-party services: payment gateways, an insurer’s quote API, review platforms and email. The quote engine is REST from front to back.
uses: API design with versioning and clear errors
Third-party integrations with retries and timeouts
Debugging the API between a front end and its data

items.name: GraphQL
items.about: GraphQL where a client needs flexible reads across many related objects, with resolvers that respect the same access rules as the REST endpoints.
uses: Batching to avoid slow nested queries

items.name: WebSockets and Socket.io
items.about: Real-time features with Socket.io: live scores pushed to thousands of fantasy sports users at once, live chat and live job status.
uses: Live updates to thousands of clients
Reconnects that do not lose state

items.name: Authentication and access control
items.about: Sign-in with email, Google and OAuth, JWT sessions, and role-based access enforced on the server. The immigration portal has client, staff and admin roles; the creator platform has 20+ community tiers.
uses: JWT sessions and sign-in shared across subdomains
Roles enforced on the server, not just hidden in the UI

items.name: Strapi
items.about: Strapi as a headless CMS when a team needs to edit content without a deploy: content models, roles and an API the front end can rely on.
uses: Strapi APIs consumed by React and mobile apps

items.name: Webhooks
items.about: Webhooks connect a product to payment providers and other services. I make every handler verify its signature and survive retries and duplicate events.
uses: Event logs for replay and debugging

items.name: Microservices
items.about: I split a system into services only where a boundary earns its cost, such as a queue-driven worker next to the main API, and keep each service small and observable.
uses: Service boundaries drawn around data ownership
Queues between services instead of chained calls

items.name: PostgreSQL
items.about: PostgreSQL is my default for SaaS data. The AI form builder, the immigration portal and the quote engine run on it, with indexes and row-level security doing real work.
uses: Normalised models with an audit trail

items.name: MySQL
items.about: MySQL for relational data in existing production systems: writing and tuning SQL, finding the slow query and keeping schemas tidy.

items.name: MongoDB
items.about: MongoDB for document data, including the creator platform’s payout ledger and referral system.
uses: A ledger as the record of every payout

items.name: DynamoDB
items.about: DynamoDB for high-throughput key-value data next to Lambda functions, with access patterns designed before the table.

items.name: Supabase
items.about: Supabase gives me Postgres, auth and storage in one place. In the AI form builder it holds every workspace’s forms, submissions and branding, isolated with row-level security.
uses: Taking over Supabase apps built with Lovable and Bolt

items.name: Redis
items.about: Redis was the quote engine’s caching layer for rate tables and partial results, part of the work that took quotes from 10+ minutes to under 2.

items.name: Firebase
items.about: Firebase for auth, real-time data and push notifications in mobile and web apps.

items.name: Row-level security
items.about: A tenant_id column only filters; one missed WHERE clause leaks data. Row-level security makes the database enforce isolation, which is how the AI form builder keeps workspaces apart.
uses: Tests that try to read another tenant’s rows

items.name: Stripe Connect
items.about: Stripe Connect runs the creator platform’s payouts: $10K+ a month, automated. Payout state lives in the platform’s own database, with Stripe as the rail, not the record.
uses: Idempotent webhook handlers for every Connect event
Payouts gated on fully verified accounts
Dunning and retries for failed charges

items.name: PayPal
items.about: PayPal was one of two payment rails on the fantasy sports platform, reconciled against Authorize.net, for real-money deposits and withdrawals.
uses: Server-side checks on every money movement

items.name: Authorize.net
items.about: Authorize.net was the second payment rail on the fantasy sports platform, behind atomic wallet operations so balances never drifted under load.
uses: Card payments for a real-money product
Fraud checks and limits on the server

items.name: AWS
items.about: Most of my production work runs on AWS, from serverless pipelines to app hosting. I hold the AWS Academy Cloud Foundations certification.
uses: Serverless architecture with Lambda, SQS and S3
Costs that idle near zero between bursts

items.name: AWS Lambda
items.about: Lambda functions do the transcoding and assembly in the video pipeline: no servers to manage, scaling with traffic for 1,000+ users.
uses: Event-driven functions from S3 and SQS

items.name: SQS
items.about: SQS is the durable job queue between upload and processing in the video pipeline, so a failed job is retried, not lost.

items.name: S3
items.about: S3 stores uploads and output in the video pipeline, and each upload triggers the next step.

items.name: Google Cloud
items.about: I support applications deployed across AWS and Google Cloud, and completed Google Cloud’s Integrate with Machine Learning APIs course.
uses: Apps that span AWS and Google Cloud

items.name: Docker
items.about: Docker keeps development, staging and production the same, so the bug you fix locally is the bug in production.

items.name: CI/CD
items.about: Every project ships through a pipeline: tests, builds and deploys on each merge, with GitHub Actions.
uses: Tests and checks on every pull request
Automated deploys to staging and production

items.name: Git
items.about: Git and code review are how I work in an existing codebase: small branches, readable commits and a decision written down in every pull request.
uses: History that explains why, not just what

items.name: Heroku
items.about: Heroku for simple hosting of Node.js apps and early-stage products that need to ship before they need their own infrastructure.
uses: Moving apps off Heroku when they outgrow it

items.name: Monitoring and debugging
items.about: I measure before I optimise. The quote engine fix started with profiling that found repeated lookups blocking every quote.
uses: Logs and alerts on errors and failed jobs
Production issue triage across front end, API and database

items.name: Amazon EC2
items.about: EC2 is for workloads that need a long-running server, such as background workers and APIs that do not fit Lambda, sized to the load and the budget.
uses: Security groups and IAM scoped tightly

items.name: Vercel
items.about: Vercel is where I host Next.js apps, with preview deployments for every pull request and environment variables kept per environment.
uses: Edge and serverless functions for Next.js

items.name: Netlify
items.about: Netlify hosts static and Jamstack sites, including this one, with builds on every push and headers and redirects kept in code.
uses: Headers and redirects in version control

items.name: React Native
items.about: React Native for iOS and Android apps that share logic and API clients with the React web app.
uses: One codebase for iOS and Android
Shared API clients with the web app

items.name: Capacitor
items.about: I shipped a cross-platform mobile app with Capacitor at QuirkBees, wrapping a web app for iOS and Android.
uses: Web apps shipped to iOS and Android
Native plugins for camera and files

items.name: iOS
items.about: I support and maintain iOS apps built with React Native and Capacitor, and troubleshoot where the app meets the API.

items.name: Android
items.about: I support and maintain Android apps built with React Native and Capacitor, from builds to Play Store releases.

items.name: Push notifications
items.about: Push and in-app notifications for status changes people care about, like a case update or a new message.
uses: Preferences so users can turn them off

items.name: Location and maps
items.about: Location capture and address fields where a workflow needs them. The AI form builder can record where a form was submitted.

items.name: Power BI
items.about: I am learning Power BI on live BI projects, building reports on top of the data the products already collect.

items.name: Jest
items.about: Jest for unit and integration tests around the code that handles money and user data, run on every pull request.
uses: Tests that run in CI on every pull request

items.name: Agile/Scrum
items.about: I run work in short sprints with clear scope, a written plan and regular demos. I led a team of five developers at 95% on-time delivery.

items.name: Jira
items.about: Jira for tracking sprints, bugs and releases in teams that already work in it.

items.name: Linear
items.about: Linear for fast, low-friction issue tracking on small product teams.

items.name: Notion
items.about: Notion for specs, decision logs and handover notes that non-technical founders can read.

items.name: Confluence
items.about: Confluence for documentation in teams that use the Atlassian suite, kept next to the Jira tickets it explains.
